finding: §3's repair picks a marker that marks the wrong release, and the corpus shows it changes nothing. §3 now says: 'tp already owns the pattern: `ReviewRound.IDScheme` plus `engine.IsLegacyRound` (`engine/reviewstate.go:503-505`) marks a round's vintage on the round itself. **`ConsecutiveCleanSince` treats a round `IsLegacyRound` reports as pre-marker the way `ConsecutiveClean` does -- no boundary -- and applies the reset only from the first marked round onward.**' Read at the cited lines, `IsLegacyRound(r) = r.IDScheme == ""`, and `engine.IDSchemeSlug` is documented in the same file (reviewstate.go:44-46) as 'the marker value recorded on a **v0.30.0+** audit round'; `audit_record.go:213` has stamped it on every audit round since. So the marker separates v0.30.0 from v0.29.0, not v0.37.0 from v0.36.0. Every audit round this release could plausibly be run against is already marked, so the reset is fully retroactive on every history that matters -- which is the exact outcome §3's next paragraph introduces the marker to prevent ('Deleting the word retroactive did not stop the mechanism being retroactive; the marker does'). Measured, not inferred: I walked all 15 recorded audit histories in spec/.tp-review/*/state.json computing ConsecutiveClean, ConsecutiveCleanSince-with-the-IsLegacyRound-check, and ConsecutiveCleanSince-without-it. **The check changes the answer in 0 of 15 histories.** v0.29.0 is the only marker-less history and its four rounds share one spec_hash, so even there the check is inert. And on v0.35.0 -- the history §3 and §2.1 both argue from -- the marked reset takes consecutive_clean from 2 to 1 (r8 hash 1259a4af, r9 hash 54e031e6, a boundary between the only two clean rounds), so §2.1's table row 'v0.35.0 | 9, converged | round 3 | round 9' is still falsified by §3 in the same file, exactly as it was before this round's repair. This is not round 4's finding restated: round 4 said prospectivity had no mechanism; this round supplied one, and the one supplied is measurably a no-op.
suggestion: `IsLegacyRound` cannot carry this. Either (a) record a NEW per-round marker written from v0.37.0 forward -- §3 may follow IDScheme's *pattern* but must not reuse its *value*, e.g. a `reset_scheme` field with `ConsecutiveCleanSince` treating an unmarked round as boundary-free -- and say plainly that this release adds a stored byte to `ReviewRound`; or (b) drop prospectivity, accept the retroactive reset, and rewrite §2.1's table under the composed rule (v0.35.0 becomes `blocking` 8 / `all` never, already simulated in §3's own paragraph) so the release's evidence and its mechanism agree. Whichever is chosen, add the assertion that discriminates: the same rounds with and without the marker must give different answers, on a fixture built for it rather than on v0.35.0's history, which cannot tell them apart.

finding: Test 10 names a killing mutation that does not kill, on the very input it names, and §5's own preamble is the standard it fails. Test 10: 'Prospectivity has a marker. A round that `engine.IsLegacyRound` reports as pre-marker contributes no boundary, so a history recorded before the upgrade keeps the `consecutive_clean` it had. The mutation that kills it: dropping the `IsLegacyRound` check, which makes v0.35.0's recorded history report `all` as never-converged.' Both halves are false against the corpus. (1) v0.35.0's nine audit rounds all carry `id_scheme: "slug"` (read from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json), so `IsLegacyRound` is false for every one of them: with the check present, v0.35.0's history ALREADY reports `all` as never-converged -- consecutive_clean falls 2 to 1 at the r8/r9 hash boundary. Dropping the check leaves that answer byte-identical, so the named mutation is not detectable on the named input. (2) 'a history recorded before the upgrade keeps the `consecutive_clean` it had' is false of the same history for the same reason: it does not keep it, it loses one. Computed across all 15 recorded audit histories, no input in this repository discriminates the two variants -- the only marker-less history, v0.29.0, has a single spec_hash across its four rounds, so the boundary rule is inert there whichever way the check goes. §5 opens 'Every test names the input that makes it fail, because four earlier drafts of this list contained a test that passed against unmodified tp'; test 10 is the fifth, and it is the test for the mechanism §3 added this round.
suggestion: Test 10 needs a fixture that is *constructed* to discriminate: two clean rounds at different `spec_hash` values with the marker absent on both (consecutive_clean stays 2) and the identical rounds with the marker present (falls to 1). State both arms in the test, since a one-arm assertion passes whatever the check does. Delete the v0.35.0 sentence, or replace it with the true statement: under §3 as written, v0.35.0's recorded history reports `all` as never-converged with the check in place, which is the finding §2.1 has to answer.

finding: The fence -- which §2 calls 'the release's actual content' -- is specified over one of the two commands that write this field, and the surface it omits is the one the guard being reversed actually exercises. §2: '`tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` with the escalation hint'; §5 test 11 repeats the same single form. tp has two workflow write surfaces and §2's own precedence chain names both layers they write: `tp set --workflow <f>=<v>` writes the task override, `tp set --workflow --project <f>=<v>` writes `.tp/config.json`. Three independent facts say the omission is live rather than pedantic. (1) The guard §4 reverses uses the project form: `internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:472` is `runTP(t, dir, "set", "--workflow", "--project", "audit_converge_on=blocking")`, so the two assertions §4 says the release reverses are assertions about the surface §2 never fences -- a unit implementing §2 and §4 literally makes `--project` succeed and leaves it unfenced. (2) The shipped mechanism already contemplates both: `fenceWorkflowWrite`'s doc comment at internal/cli/unattended.go:50-55 says 'so both tp set --workflow and its --project form can call it on every field they parse', and the shipped `runner`/`notify_cmd` fence is 'at **any** layer' (REFERENCE.md's fence table). (3) The twin's own shipped spec covers both by name: spec/0.31.0.md:41 -- 'Both `tp set --workflow review_converge_on=<bad>` and `tp set --workflow --project review_converge_on=<bad>` validate the literal value they are about to persist'. So this release specifies a fence narrower than the precedent it cites, on the release whose stated purpose is that fence, and the gap is a supported route for an unattended unit to relax its own audit gate -- 'the failure the whole unattended-mode design exists to prevent', in §2's words. The same one-surface narrowness leaves the validation contract short: §2 says only 'rejected with the same hint machinery', while spec/0.31.0.md:41 splits exit 2 (a value on the command line) from exit 1 (a hand-edited stored layer a consuming command resolves), and §5 test 1 asserts only 'the same hint shape'.
suggestion: Write the fence over both forms -- '`tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` both exit 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`' -- and make test 11 assert both arms plus the exit-0 arm without the variable. Take spec/0.31.0.md:41's exit-code split for the invalid-value path as well, since 'the same hint machinery' does not say which code, and name `.tp/config.json` as a fenced layer explicitly so the implementer does not have to infer it from the field list.

finding: §2's justification for the fence rests on a superlative its own next paragraph refutes. §2: 'This is the **first workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate**; `review_converge_on`'s weak value is its own default, so nothing has needed this before.' Two sentences later: 'the only workflow-write fence is `fenceWorkflowWrite(field string, requested float64)` in `internal/cli/unattended.go:56` -- **numeric by signature**, covering caps and command fields.' A cap fence exists precisely because raising a cap relaxes a gate. Verified in the shipped surface: `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`'s fence table carries '`tp set --workflow review_max_rounds=` / `audit_max_rounds=` **above** the resolved value | exit 2' and the same row for `run_max_*`, and REFERENCE.md's own explanation is 'an equal or lower value is accepted and exits 0, since lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence' -- i.e. the raise is the relaxation. `review_max_rounds`, `audit_max_rounds` and the five `run_max_*` fields are all workflow fields whose non-default value relaxes a gate, and all seven are already fenced. The clause that IS true and that carries the whole mechanical argument is the narrower one: this is the first **string-valued** such field, which is exactly why a `float64` signature does not fit it. As written the sentence overstates the release's novelty, and it does so in the paragraph that answers 'why is the fence the content of this release' -- so a reader who checks the superlative finds it false and has no reason left for the paragraph. It also invites the wrong repair: 'widen the fence to string fields' reads as inventing a category when the category already exists and only its parameter type is wrong.
suggestion: Write 'the first **string-valued** workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate -- the seven cap fields already do, which is why `fenceWorkflowWrite` exists, and why its `float64` parameter is the whole problem'. That keeps the argument, makes it true, and names the fix as a signature change rather than a new concept.

finding: The sentence this round added to close a precedence finding is itself an uncounted uniqueness claim, and it is wrong in all three of its parts. §2: 'The five-layer form is still written in `CLAUDE.md`, which is where this draft copied it from; that is fixed with this release.' (1) Present tense, false: CLAUDE.md no longer carries it. Read at CLAUDE.md:327-332, the line now says 'effective values **resolve at read time** (**task override > project config > built-in** -- there is no CLI layer and no `TP_<FIELD>` environment layer for a workflow field ... This line carried the five-layer form until v0.37.0's review round 4)'. `git log -- CLAUDE.md` shows it repaired in 975a1b8, 'docs: correct the precedence chain at its source' -- before this round. (2) 'still written in CLAUDE.md' is an exhaustiveness claim over a set nobody enumerated, and two live locations survive. `grep -rln 'CLI > env > task override'` outside spec/.tp-review/ returns spec/0.31.0.md and spec/0.35.0.md; spec/0.35.0.md's is the historical note §2 already cites, but **spec/0.31.0.md:41 is a live normative sentence about the twin field itself** -- '`review_converge_on` resolves like every other workflow field (CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in default)'. A reader sent to the twin for the pattern lands on the five-layer form. (3) Worse, one of the two files §2's own cost paragraph puts in this release's scope states the phantom layer as fact: `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:327-328` -- 'Under the variable the **env layer** of the precedence (`TP_RUN_MAX_UNITS`, `TP_REVIEW_MAX_ROUNDS`, ...) is ignored for every fenced field.' Neither variable exists: I enumerated every `TP_[A-Z_]*` literal in non-test internal/ and cmd/ code and the list is TP_ESCALATION_PATH, TP_FAKE_RUNNER_*, TP_FILE, TP_HC, TP_PHASE, TP_ROUND, TP_ROUND_DIR, TP_RUN_DIR, TP_RUN_ID, TP_RUNNER, TP_RUNNER_SEAM, TP_STOP_REASON, TP_UNATTENDED, TP_UNIT_ID, TP_UNIT_KIND, TP_UNIT_SEQ -- no TP_RUN_MAX_UNITS, no TP_REVIEW_MAX_ROUNDS. So the release claims a documentation repair that was already made, and misses the two places the same error is still live, one of them in its own declared scope.
suggestion: Replace with what is true and counted: 'CLAUDE.md carried the five-layer form until this cycle's review round 4 and was corrected at 975a1b8. Two live statements of it remain and this release corrects both: spec/0.31.0.md:41, which states it normatively of `review_converge_on` itself, and skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:327-328, which names `TP_RUN_MAX_UNITS` and `TP_REVIEW_MAX_ROUNDS` as an env layer that no code reads.' Then add a §5 test or a `workflow.checks` entry that greps the repository for the five-layer string, because this is the third round the claim has been restated from memory rather than counted.

finding: Non-Goal 6 defers a deliverable on the strength of a counted cost, and the count is inflated by half. §4: 'The review side emits `nonblocking_open` (`review_record.go:231`) and six places -- `spec/0.31.0.md` §8.4, `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:634`, `skills/tp/SKILL.md`, `reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205`, `harness_note_test.go:263` and 0.31.0's test 18 -- pin its absence on the audit side **by name**. Creating the counterpart means inverting a pinned guard.' Two of the six pin nothing. `harness_note_test.go:263` is a **comment line** -- '// next_action retained (§8.4). nonblocking_open is review-only and never here.' -- inside `TestCompact_AuditOmitsHarnessKeepsNextAction`, and I read that function end to end (lines 264-299): it asserts on harness_stale, harness_note and next_action and contains no assertion mentioning `nonblocking_open` at all. Adding the audit-side field would not turn it red. `skills/tp/SKILL.md` names `nonblocking_open` at exactly two lines, 72 and 76, both inside Workflow B (review); its audit sections, lines 146-147, enumerate the audit `--status` fields and never mention the field, so SKILL.md does not pin its absence 'by name' -- it simply does not mention it, which is the opposite of a pin and costs nothing to change. Four real pins remain: spec/0.31.0.md §8.4 and test 18, REFERENCE.md:634 ('review-only'), and reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205, which is the only executable one. The direction of the error is what makes it worth reporting: an inflated cost is being used to justify not shipping an observable §4 itself argues an agent needs ('an agent reading `clean: true` cannot tell an empty round from a suppressed one'), on the release that creates the suppression. And the wrong figure has already propagated -- spec/0.46.0.md:330 carries 'six places pin its **absence** on the audit side', so the receiving spec will inherit it.
suggestion: Say four, and separate them by kind: 'two shipped spec clauses (spec/0.31.0.md §8.4 and test 18), one documented field disposition (REFERENCE.md:634), and one executable assertion (reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205, which is the only one that turns red).' Drop harness_note_test.go:263 (a comment) and skills/tp/SKILL.md (silence, not a pin). Correct spec/0.46.0.md:330 in the same edit, since it is already carrying the number forward.

finding: The release introduces a field it repeatedly calls the twin of `review_converge_on` -- identical name shape, identical value vocabulary, 'this is its twin' -- whose default is the opposite of the twin's, and never says so. Verified at `internal/engine/configresolve.go:243`: the built-in default layer sets `ReviewConvergeOn: ReviewConvergeOnBlocking`, and reviewconvergeon.go:8-9 gives the two constants as `blocking`/`all`. So `review_converge_on` ships at `blocking` (the permissive value) while §2 sets `audit_converge_on` to `all` (the strict value). After this release `tp config --resolved` prints the two adjacently as `review_converge_on: blocking` and `audit_converge_on: all`, and an operator or agent reading them as a matched pair reads the audit loop as the *lenient* one. §2 says only 'Default: `all`. The behaviour tp ships today, so no existing project changes' -- true, and it does not mention that the same words mean opposite postures on the two fields. This is not the earlier round's finding that the default was stated as `blocking` matching review; the default has since changed to `all` and the unstated thing is now the divergence itself. It also loads §2's fence argument: '`review_converge_on`'s weak value is its own default, so nothing has needed this before' is exactly this asymmetry, stated as a fact about the fence without ever being stated as a fact about the two defaults a reader will see side by side.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §2 under 'Default: `all`': 'Note the two fields default oppositely -- `review_converge_on` ships at `blocking` (configresolve.go:243) and `audit_converge_on` at `all` -- so the shared vocabulary does not mean shared strictness; §2.1 is why, and it is the reason this field, unlike its twin, needs a fence.' Consider having `tp config --resolved`'s documentation in REFERENCE.md carry the same note, since that surface is where the two appear together.

finding: §3's call-site enumeration is now complete but not uniformly precise, and the one site it leaves imprecise is the only phase-shared one. It gives line numbers for the two sites whose phase is load-bearing (`resume.go:87`, `review_status.go:67`) and bare filenames for the rest: '`Converged` is reached from `audit_record.go` (twice), `run_status.go`, `budget.go`'. I checked all of them: audit_record.go:95 and :333 are audit-only, run_status.go:149 is audit-only (it reads `st.AuditRounds`), resume.go:86 is the review half correctly excluded, and review_report.go:106 calls a local `isConverged` over `roundStats` rather than `engine.Converged`, so the list is not short. But `budget.go:26` is different in kind from every other entry: `refuseIfBudgetExhausted(kind, ...)` computes `converged := engine.Converged(...)` unconditionally at :26 and then, at :28, overwrites it with `engine.ReviewConverged(...)` when `kind == "review"`. One statement, both phases, discriminated by a runtime branch rather than by which file it sits in. Swapping it to `ConvergedSince` therefore executes on the review path too -- harmlessly, since the value is discarded two lines later, but a decomposer reading '`budget.go`' in a list §3 introduces with 'Every call site, enumerated, because two enumerations of this list have already been short' has no way to know that this entry needs the branch read before it is touched, and Non-Goal 4's promise ('review's `--status` cannot move') is what makes that reading necessary.
suggestion: Give it the same treatment as the two sites §3 already pins: '`budget.go:26`, which is phase-shared -- the unconditional call is overwritten at :28 by `ReviewConverged` when `kind == "review"`, so the audit branch is the only consumer and the substitution is safe.' One clause, and it converts the entry from something a task must re-derive into something a task's acceptance can state.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught, two halves of the same shape. (1) I was about to file '§3's `Converged` enumeration is short again -- it omits `resume.go:86` and `review_report.go:106`, and its own sentence says two earlier enumerations were short.' Both would have been wrong. `internal/engine/resume.go:86` is `reviewConverged := Converged(reviewRounds, ...)` -- the review half of an adjacent pair, correctly excluded by a section whose subject is the audit path, and §3 cites :87 precisely to distinguish them. `internal/cli/review_report.go:106` is `converged := isConverged(rounds)`, a file-local helper over `[]roundStats` declared at :317, not `engine.Converged` at all. Enumerated properly, `engine.Converged` has exactly the seven non-test callers §3 implies and names the right six. (2) I was about to file 'test 9 is wrong that `review_status.go:91`'s `consecutive_clean` still reports 3, because review convergence is severity-aware and goes through `ReviewConsecutiveClean`.' Also wrong: review_status.go:91 genuinely calls plain `engine.ConsecutiveClean(rounds)`; it is review_record.go:204, review.go:979/:1940 and import_enforce.go:51 that use `ReviewConsecutiveClean`. That review `--status` and review `--record` compute the same field by different predicates is real and is a pre-existing asymmetry this release neither creates nor touches -- not a §3 defect. Recording both because the class is the one this cycle keeps producing in the other direction: a section that has been wrong about a list before reads as wrong about the list now, and what separated the two here was enumerating the callers rather than trusting the section's own history.
suggestion: No spec change. If §3 wants the point made permanently, the enumeration is now checkable: a `workflow.checks` entry that greps for `engine.Converged(` and `ConsecutiveClean(` in non-test internal/ code and compares the file:line set against §3's list would catch the next short enumeration without a reviewer re-deriving it, and this section has now cost three rounds of exactly that.
